answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate most directions before the memory even matters. Rollback is ruled out by compliance (memory_b1 is the strongest-looking precedent and is simply unavailable). Circuit breakers (memory_b4) fail fast by design — that contained a partner outage where shedding was acceptable, but here shedding at settlement peak means dropping exactly the customer writes the objective says to protect. Regional failover (memory_b2) moved a latency problem cleanly, but that was a read-heavy degradation; cutting regions mid-peak with heavy writes risks in-flight write loss and replication-lag divergence, which is the one failure mode I cannot undo. Add capacity (memory_b3) worked when provisioned *before* a known peak; provisioning now is slow to take effect and does nothing if the bottleneck is primary-node contention rather than raw headroom. That leaves read-replica routing (memory_b5), which is the only reversible, write-preserving lever: it reduces contention on the primary rather than redistributing or discarding traffic. I am spending the single verification on memory_b5 precisely because it is the memory I intend to act on and it is the one whose applicability I am least able to check from the summary. The summary asserts a same-day recovery but not causation — I need the original record to see whether the primary's load was actually dominated by report/dashboard queries, whether the change was made under peak write load or in a quiet window, and whether anything else changed concurrently. Two things would break the inference: if the current latency climb originates in the 2-hour-old release rather than read contention, offloading reads treats the wrong cause; and if report volume is a small fraction of primary load today, the intervention is a no-op that burns my one window. Hence small_guarded_test: route a limited slice of report/analytics queries first, watch p99 on the write path and replica lag, and expand only on a clear signal. Explicit downstream risk: consumers of routed queries begin reading lagged data, and any settlement or reconciliation logic that silently assumes read-after-write consistency could compute wrong figures during peak — that must be flagged to compliance and finance rather than absorbed quietly. Also noting the release timing correlation remains unexplained and unaddressed; if verification undercuts memory_b5, add_capacity becomes the fallback, and the release-induced hypothesis needs escalation in the next window since rollback is off the table.
